If one does not take the final mantra as the primary teaching, then within each of the first three mantras, one may designate them as either primary or auxiliary, thereby likewise attaining the sense of both the general and the specific.
Now, regarding the first incantation, it is divided into five parts:

first, exhorting the three karmas as the causal basis; second, praising the essence and function of the incantation; third, the actual recitation of the incantation; fourth, clarifying the benefits gained by the practitioner; and fifth, the restoration of the afflicted person to health.
The exhortation to the responsive capacity is twofold:
first, the narrative by the scriptural author; second, the formal invocation through the three karmas.

The triple invocation of the Triple Gem serves as a general locus for the pacification and subjugation of afflictions for all sentient beings, whereas Avalokiteśvara is the specific object of focus. Therefore, the invocation of the Triple Gem possesses both a general and a specific dimension, which is why the threefold invocation is employed.
It may be that three recitations are required in order to eliminate the three obstructions, or to manifest the three cycles of the incantation’s exposition, or to represent the three explanations;
thus, the three karmas are as stated in the text, and so forth.
The four lines of verse are divided into two parts:
the first two lines constitute the formal request, and the latter two lines constitute the concluding request.
The first part is further divided into two:
The first line is a general invitation, while the second line is a specific invitation.
The first phrase indicates the self-invitation; the subsequent three phrases indicate both self-invitation and invitation by others.
Regarding "those in distress," it refers to the ten types of practitioners, all of whom are said to be in distress, and so forth.
It is not only that suffering resides in the body, such as the calamities of bloodshot eyes and pus-filled ears.
That Great Compassion covers all beings does not merely mean it covers the sufferings within the city of Śrāvastī; it also covers those within the ten dharma realms, which is why it is called "all."
"Universally emitting light" means requesting the light of great wisdom for the purpose of subduing and harmonizing; thus, the darkness of ignorance and delusion is extinguished and eliminated.
As stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, it further emits light to eliminate various objects of treatment, such as stinginess, anger, and so forth.
Now, this light of wisdom also cures the toxic harms of the ten types of practitioners.
When ignorance is exhausted, it is like covering the great earth, whereby delusions are immediately and suddenly eliminated;
when the delusions of the ten persons are eliminated in succession, it is the gradual elimination of delusions.
Next is the specific invitation, which specifically designates the three obstacles.
"The suffering of killing" refers to the poisonous harm of evil karma.

Because of this poisonous harm, one invites retribution in the form of suffering; therefore, it is called "harm. This explains the poisonous harm of evil karma throughout the ten types of practitioners.

Just as Māra joyfully comes to harass the practitioner, or brings forth emptiness to destroy their cultivation within existence, causing them to fall into the two vehicles and harming the goodness of their bodhi.
Or, one might bring forth scattered wholesome acts such as giving, which destroy the wholesome qualities of emptiness, signlessness, and outflowlessness, causing one to fall among humans and devas.
All of these are harmful to the true meaning.
The two obstacles are as described in the text.
"Surely he will come to bestow great bliss" means that he requests Great Compassion, for Great Compassion tames, harmonizes, and brings about great bliss.
The former [Great Pity] uproots suffering; this is the sense of "extinguishing.
Furthermore, if the retribution of worldly suffering is removed, it is also called "bliss," and the successful accomplishment of the virtues of humans and devas is likewise called "bliss."

While such states as these possess a sense of pleasure, they are not termed "Great"; only upon attaining the principle of the Perfect Teaching (Pūrṇa-yāna) of eternal bliss can it be called "Great Bliss.
Since the request made was for long-lasting speech, we know that the request did not pertain merely to the single instance of retributive suffering in the city of Śrāvastī.
Regarding the next two verses that address the "compassionate father": those of ten types of practitioners are all termed the "world of sentient beings.
That they possess the relationship of father and son means that they equally possess Buddha-nature.
The principle of the *tathāgatagarbha* is the nature of the direct cause (*hetu-pratyaya*).

Having followed one another through past lives, having performed various meritorious deeds, and having followed the path of transformation by bowing the head and raising the hands—this is the nature of the conditional cause (*pratyaya-pratyaya*).

However, although the enabling cause (了因) was previously absent, now that the bonds have been extinguished, it is said that the poisonous harm has been eliminated and restored to its original state; is this not the nature of the enabling cause?
Because the three types of innate natures are interconnected, one can become father and son.
Therefore, the prayer says: "O Compassionate Father of the World, relieve me from the suffering of the three poisons.
One should know that this request for a father is exceedingly vast; how could it merely refer to the obstacles to karmic retribution within this single lifetime?
The removal of illness constitutes happiness in the present life; attaining the Path in the future constitutes the happiness of Nirvana.
Within the future, Nirvana with remainder constitutes happiness in the present life, while Nirvana without remainder constitutes happiness in the future life.
Ten kinds of people shall attain the Path as their present life and ultimate Nirvana as their future life.
All other forms of happiness are not the Great Happiness; only the ultimate state is the Great Happiness.
The second section is the praise of the divine mantra, which is twofold:
first, praising the essence of the mantra; second, clarifying its function.
From the words "He addressed the Buddha" up to "certainly," this constitutes the praise of the essence.

This is the essence of the true mark of correct contemplation, which is neither empty nor existent; it obstructs the evil karma of the two extremes and upholds the right goodness of the Middle Way, and is thus named the essence of the True Mark Mantra.
This essence possesses the three virtues, neither vertical nor horizontal.
The text states: "The dharani-seal of all Buddhas of the three periods is precisely the virtue of the dharmakaya’s true mark;
it is necessarily the lion’s roar, definitively expounding prajna."
"Auspiciousness" means that all sufferings are forever brought to an end, universally causing each to attain liberation.
These three virtues are used to praise the essence of the dhāraṇī.
Furthermore, "Certainty" is named after the lion's roar, in the sense of eliminating and uprooting suffering.
"Śrī" (Auspiciousness) is a term for virtuous benefit; it signifies the meaning of subduing and bliss.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "This is the great divine mantra, the great timely mantra, the peerless mantra."

"Mantras are simply vows. When the Buddha preached the Dharma, he vowed that sentient beings would be as established by these mantras; they are like the larvae of the *mingling* (the caterpillars of the *long-ling* wasp). Therefore, all sutras are mantras."

The mantra of the Middle Way obstructs the two extremes by subduing emptiness and subduing existence; it destroys the two extremes by extinguishing emptiness and extinguishing existence—this is what is meant by "eliminating and subduing.
There are also further nuances such as "remaining subdual" (yu-fu) and "level subdual" (ping-fu), and so forth.

Mantras are also vows, as well as prohibitions and oaths; they are also incantations and ritual arts. These arts and methods are entirely bestowed upon those who practice the ten stages of conduct; they correspond to the subduing of poisons and harms, secretly capable of eliminating and suppressing them. These secret essentials of all Buddhas are inconceivable.
The seal of the Buddhas of the three periods is the Seal of True Reality (dharmatā-mudrā); it certifies all sutras and is therefore called the essence of the mantra.
To hear this mantra is itself its manifest application.
If one does not recognize a medicine, one does not yet know its excellence;
if one does not understand how to use it, how can one know its potency?

The exhaustion of suffering is extinction (*kṣaya*); the attainment of happiness is subduing (*dāma*). To distance oneself from the eight difficulties is extinction; to attain the concentration of mindfulness of the Buddha is subduing. Subduing brings about gentleness and goodness.
To perceive various Buddhas, or even to have views of existence and non-existence—these four views, which are reckoned perversely and do not accord with principle, are all called evil karma.

What is seen by the Two Vehicles within emptiness, as well as the four gates of the Tripiṭaka Teaching and the four gates of the Shared Teaching, all fail to accord with principle and are likewise evil karma. Now, this divine mantra of the Middle Way can completely eliminate and subdue them; one should know that the spiritual efficacy of this mantra is vast and far-reaching.
Fourth, the holder attains merit, as stated in the text.
Fifth, "restored to its original state" refers to the ten types of practitioners being clarified as having returned to their original nature;
this refers to the illness of ignorance within the *saṃbhogakāya*, which is now cured and restored to its original state.

Having originally cultivated the mind of worldly goodness, one is free from the harm of evil karma and the afflictions of the five sensory objects; now, returning once more to the wholesome roots of humans and devas, one cultivates the Four Noble Truths to seek Nirvana.
Because one was previously free from views and cravings, and now has attained the prior mind, it is said to be "restored.

This applies even to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao): its essence is originally the pure illumination of the Dharma-nature (dharmatā). When the disease of the delusive afflictions of the five abodes arises, once that disease is eliminated, it is identical to the Dharma-nature; therefore, it is said to be "as it was originally."
Second, from "At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion" onwards is the mantra for destroying evil karma.
This section is divided into three parts:
first, the Tathāgata’s earnest request; second, Avalokiteśvara’s compliance with the command and his discourse; third, the Buddha’s confirmation and completion.
Now, as for the mention of "the Buddha’s request," this is not a request made by himself, but rather one made for the sake of protecting the Dharma on behalf of others.

The character "qǐng" (request) has two pronunciations; if it is used in its refined (jìngyǔ) form, it may be applied to those of lower rank, such as when a Son of Heaven requests his hundred officials.
Furthermore, the title of the sutra refers to it as "Pure" (Jing), which may be applied to ordinary people; however, if one uses the term "invocation" (qing), it becomes redundant.
These two terms should be adjusted according to the context.
My current intention in repeating the phrase "incantation for eliminating and subduing poisonous harm" is to speak from a general perspective.
Furthermore, regarding the mantra for destroying evil karma, it is designated separately as before, and so forth.
Second, the actual exposition of the mantra is divided into two parts:
First, the actual recitation of the mantra; second, the clarification of its power and function.
Regarding the first, the phrase "relying upon the Buddha's power" means relying upon the power of the Great Enlightenment of Suchness (tathatā).
To further invoke the Triple Gem, the meaning is the same as previously explained.
"All fears" is further divided into two parts:
first, a general explanation of the power and function of the mantra; second, a detailed exposition.
Regarding "all fears" mentioned here: first, it refers to the fact that throughout the ten types of practitioners, each possesses their own specific fears.

Second, regarding those who become evil spirits, tigers, or wolves: for example, in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, from the first bhūmi through the tenth bhūmi, there are all manner of perils involving tigers, wolves, and lions.
Among these, the ten types of persons are tigers and wolves in the midst of non-affairs; they are designated as tigers and wolves with respect to the phenomena of affliction (*kleśa*).
Regarding the specific explanation, it begins from "those who violate those who practice the holy life" (*brahmacārin*).

Regarding the ten unwholesome actions (*daśākuśalakarmapatha*): these ten unwholesome acts are natural precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*); they constitute offenses whether one has formally undertaken them or not, unlike other types of prohibitive or restrictive precepts (*pratikṣepaṇa-śīla*).
For example, regarding the precept concerning grass and trees for a *bhikṣu*, one incurs an offense if one has undertaken it, but does not incur an offense if one has not.
Now, regarding those whose natures are heavy, the power of the mantra can cause them to become pure; for those whose natures are light, they are extinguished by analogy.
As for "if" (shè), there are two meanings:
first, hypothetical "if"; second, merely "if."

The principle of intrinsic purity is fundamentally free from evil karma; the evil karma that now arises is entirely false and illusory. Since reality comes to shatter the illusory and renders all things pure, it is said "even if" (or "should there be").
This clarifies the provisional nature of the removal of delusions.

As for the phrase "merely established," it means that if there is even a single phenomenon subsumed under the category of karma—regardless of whether it is grave or light—this mantra is capable of destroying it all and rendering it pure.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "Even if there were a single dharma that transcended nirvāṇa, it would likewise be like an illusion or a transformation.
This passage clearly asserts non-existence, just as the nineteenth sense-field (*āyatana*) and so forth are ultimately unobtainable.

Now, as for what is called "provisional assumption," it does not preclude the existence of fleeting pleasure; this is similar to the "provisional discourse" (*prajñapti-vāda*) in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, yet it differs from it in various ways.
Those who see the Buddha in the present take the samādhi of seeing the Buddha as the seed.

When those in the hells contemplate the Buddha, the perceived manifestations of his form and substance differ; even among humans, what is seen by ordinary beings, those of the Two Vehicles, and the various Bodhisattvas—whether common or distinct—each differs.
In general, there are approximately ten types of practitioners who perceive the Buddha differently, and their methods of samādhi contemplation likewise vary, and so forth.
From the point where the Buddha addresses Ānanda onwards, this constitutes the third section: the Buddha’s confirmation and elaboration.

This is divided into four parts: first, describing its efficacy; second, exhorting the practice of the method and procedure; third, citing scriptural evidence; and fourth, concluding with the description of its efficacy.

Regarding the explanation of its efficacy, it is able to eliminate two kinds of afflictions: freedom from physical suffering and freedom from mental illness. From the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) up to the level of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), as long as one remains within a single lifetime, both body and mind are present.

Within the realm of segmented existence (*paricchinna-bhava*), one possesses the body and mind of the three miserable realms; for humans, there is physical illness up to the fourth dhyāna, while in the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*), there is mental illness. Thus, one knows that suffering and pleasure follow the body up to the fourth dhyāna, whereas grief and joy follow the mind up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

If a śrāvaka among those who practice the five stages of expedient means is fully possessed of physical and mental afflictions, then although a srotāpanna has seen the truths, the stage of contemplation still remains; even for an arhat, residual temporal bodies and illnesses still persist, and the non-forgetting of habitual tendencies is likewise a mental affliction.
It is the same for the Pratyekabuddhas;
it is also the same for the general teaching of the six perfections.

If one cuts off birth in the *pariccheda* (segmented) realm to undergo *pariṇāma* (transformation), this refers to the depth, shallowness, superiority, and inferiority of the fivefold Dharma-body within the Four Truths of Non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*), as well as the heaviness or lightness of the mental afflictions residing in the ground of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*), up until the point where only one more birth remains.
The abiding of the three sages and ten saints in their karmic retribution—is this not the body?

Even up to the desire to attain the unsurpassed retribution of Buddhahood, all of it is a bodily affliction as long as ignorance is not yet exhausted; that the Buddha-nature is not realized is entirely a mental illness.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "By the cessation of this form, one attains eternal form," and only then is there no physical illness.

"By the cessation of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, one attains eternal feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness," and only then is there no mental illness.
Furthermore, regarding these two afflictions of body and mind, they are categorized according to the ten types of practitioners, and so forth.
Fire coming from the four directions is external fire;
pain in every joint is internal fire.
The explanation of the facts follows the text.
Regarding "understanding as coming from without": this refers to the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) which arise from arbitrary conceptualization; therefore, it is said to come from without.
"The four sides" refers to the four views of existence, non-existence, and so forth.
Because this view incinerates the understanding of the truths (*satyadarśana*), it is said that "the body is burned.

The dragon is a divine and spiritual being, representing the Dharma King; its spontaneous establishment of teachings is like the rain from a dragon, and its extinguishing of the delusions of views is like fire being put out—this refers to one who practices through faith (*śraddhānusārin*).
Pain in every joint refers to the afflictions of conceptualization (*vitarka-kleśa*).

It arises from attachment to principles; for example, a person who has attained the realization of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) understanding, such as a *srotāpanna*, still possesses afflictions of conceptualization, and therefore it is called "internal fire."
"Segment by segment" refers to the nine grades to be abandoned through contemplation.
Are not the nine grades of the desire realm, as well as those of the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments in each respective location, indeed "segment by segment"?
Previously, when one practiced faith and conduct, the dragon king sent down rain.
Now, the dragon is none other than the uncontaminated mind-king; by giving rise to the dharma-water of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), it extinguishes the fire of afflictions of thought.

This explanation is based on ten types of practitioners; the *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (segmented cessation) of *dṛṣṭi-āsrava* (afflictions of views) and *bhāvanā-āsrava* (afflictions of cultivation) can be understood accordingly.

Since the *parinirmita-vaiśvāsika* (transformational) realm possesses the superior and wondrous five desires of Bodhisattvas, within this state there naturally exists the "unconditioned" (*anabhisaṃskāra*) *dṛṣṭi-āsrava* and *bhāvanā-āsrava* beyond the [three] realms. Applying the analogy of fire, this extends up to the stage of "one more birth" (*ekajātipratibaddha*), and so forth.
Regarding "the price of grain being high and famine occurring": the explanation of the matter is that when the five grains are not harvested, it is called famine;
when vegetables do not grow, it is called scarcity. To explain by analogy: being far from the Sage and not hearing the Way is famine;
being near [to the Sage] is satiety. Lacking right wisdom is famine; lacking the factors conducive to the Path is scarcity.
As in the *Lotus Sūtra* regarding those who are "hungry, emaciated, and weak," this refers to the level of phenomena (*vastu*).
Even the virtues of humans and devas are all analogous to the meaning of hunger and satiety.
If the followers of the two vehicles were not hungry, the *Lotus Sūtra* would not have said that they came from a land of hunger.

This means that the Hīnayāna is for those who are hungry, while the Mahāyāna is for those who are satiated; this is according to the tradition passed down by ten people, and so forth. Regarding the "King's Obstacles":

in the stage of segmented existence (*pariccheda*), the four Māras are used as obstacles; in the stage of transformation (*pariṇāma*), the ten Māras are used as obstacles. Since there are even Māras within the stage of a single lifetime (*ekajāti-pratibaddha*), it is said that although the three Māras have been exhausted, only a portion of the Māra of Death (*mṛtyu-māra*) remains.
The wild beasts are evil karma; the thieves are the six sense organs and the six sense objects; losing one’s way is heterodoxy; and the prison is retribution.
There are two kinds of retribution:
first, the retribution-prison as explained in relation to the various realms of existence, such as when a person attains heaven and so forth.
Second, one receives a body within the prison according to one's respective lot.

This is also categorized according to the ten types of practitioners: handcuffs and fetters represent obstacles to concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*); the pillory represents obstacles to the provisional and the ultimate; and the chains represent the cords of karma and so forth that bind one to rebirth.
The ocean is birth-and-death, or it is called the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature), because deluded conceptualization moves the *dharmatā*.
The waves represent the perils; the yakṣas and rākṣasas represent views and afflictions (*kleśa*); and the poisonous medicine represents the realm of principle.
Just as the four types of views (dṛṣṭi) are rendered poisonous when they are logically untenable, so too is the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) called both a poison and nectar.
Swords and blades are impermanent; the three realms are all subject to the transience of impermanence, and so forth.
Second, from this point until the consecration of the dhāraṇī, there is the exhortation to practice according to the Dharma.
This section has three parts:
first, the formal exhortation; second, the demonstration of the application of the method; and third, the attainment of benefits.
Regarding "consecration" (*abhiṣeka*), the commentary explains the matter as follows:

when a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) intends to invest his crown prince with the throne, he takes the waters of the four oceans and pours them over the prince’s head, entrusting him with the entire world; hence it is called "consecration."

According to the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, when the Buddha bestows the prediction of enlightenment upon a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage, he sprinkles the water of the ocean of *dharmatā* upon the crown of the Dharma Prince of the tenth stage; this is called "receiving office from the Buddha," and is therefore termed "consecration" (*abhiṣeka*).
Now this meaning is clarified:
there are ten kinds of persons whose wisdom can see the crown of the head;
the Buddha, however, is the Dharma-nature itself, and none can see his crown.
When others possess only a small portion of wisdom and are utterly unable to fathom the ultimate principle, it is called the "Summit" (mūrdhan).

If they receive the empowerment through the bestowal of *dhāraṇī* mantras, they are then able to advance toward realization and their practice becomes ever deeper; this is called "Empowerment" (abhiṣeka).
Thus, with respect to these ten types of persons, each possesses the meaning of a "summit" (*mūrdhan*) and each possesses the meaning of being "sprinkled.

Only the body of the Subtle Enlightenment (*sūkṣma-bodhi*), being supreme and ultimate, cannot be sprinkled further; yet it is able to universally sprinkle the summits of the ten types of persons with the water of the *dhāraṇī*. This is the summit of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
"Fasting" (zhāi) means "to align" (qí); it is the alignment of the karma of body and speech. This alignment is simply the Middle Way.
The prohibition against eating thereafter symbolizes that beyond the Dharma-realm of the Middle Way, there is no other separate dharma.
That one obtains a morsel before midday, rather than at the exact midpoint, clearly indicates the preceding preparatory stage (*pūrvaprayoga*).

However, within that which resembles the Path (*mārga*), there is the sense of attaining realization; thus, one obtains a morsel. This also signifies that, outside of the Middle Way Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), there exists further phenomena.
Not eating meat is the great compassion that is without conditions; therefore, one does not eat it.

Compassion based on sentient beings (*sattvālambana*) and compassion based on phenomena (*dharmālambana*) both have limitations, whereas this compassion without conditions has no limitations; thus, one must not eat it.
The ashes represent the five contemplations for settling the mind (*pañca-vastu-sthāpana*).
The five pungent, bitter, and spicy flavors represent the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
The odor of raw meat represents the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*) within the five aggregates.
"Defilement" refers to the suffering and accumulation of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
"The Buddhas of the ten directions" means that within all ten dharma-realms there is Buddha-nature.
"The seven Buddhas" refers to the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*).
Third, the passage beginning with the Buddha’s address to Ānanda regarding a woman who departed serves as a scriptural citation (*pramāṇa*).
It is not a solitary proof; this section also corroborates what preceded it, as indicated by the text at length.
Fourth: From this point, the three obstructions are eternally exhausted through the merit of this mantra; this is the function of its completion, as stated in the text.
Third: From the passage "If there are sentient beings in prison," this is the third section of the mantra that eliminates the obstruction of retribution.
This consists of four parts:
first, clarifying the缘由 (causes and conditions) for reciting the mantra; second, the actual recitation of the mantra; third, praising its efficacy; and fourth, the conclusion.
Regarding the first, the causes and conditions, and the second, the actual recitation, they are as stated in the text.
The third section praises the efficacy [of the six-syllable mantra], which consists of three parts:

first, clarifying the efficacy of the six-character phrases regarding the six realms of existence; second, clarifying the efficacy of the six-character phrases regarding the cultivation of causes; and third, clarifying the efficacy of the six-character phrases regarding the six sense faculties.
Regarding his explanation of the "six words," some say that reciting the names of the Triple Gem constitutes these six-word phrases.
This allocation of the six words is indeed sufficient; however, one does not see within the text any statement marking the sections or concluding the phrases.
Alternatively, one may take "Three Jewels" as three characters, or "Avalokiteśvara" as three characters; this is convenient for recitation and retention.

Since the preceding passage did not specify the concluding phrases of each section, if one uses these six characters, they will be present everywhere, and thus the meaning will be universally applicable.
Now, none of these [previous methods] are employed.

Regarding the clarification of the six-character phrases here, although the scriptural text contains headings, concluding sentences, and passages marking the beginning and end, we clarify the six-character phrases for the sake of convenience in explaining the meaning.
Now, examining the sūtras in relation to the six destinies, the six subtle gates, the six sense organs, and so forth, we clarify the meaning of the six-character phrases.
This is like the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, which correlates the twenty-five states of existence with the twenty-five samādhis.
Now, by clarifying the six-character phrases in relation to the six realms of existence, one achieves the subduing and elimination of the harmful poisons of those six realms.
For this reason, these three types of phrases are elucidated as being convenient for the purpose.
Regarding these three kinds of six-syllable phrases, there are three instances where they appear:
first, concerning the six-syllable chapter that clarifies karmic retribution, it states immediately after the completion of the verse:
"If any members of the fourfold assembly hear these six-syllable phrases," and then proceeds to explain extensively the efficacy of uprooting suffering within the six realms of existence.
The concluding verse states:
"If there are those who hear these six-syllable phrases.
Next, regarding the explanation of the six-syllable phrases for cultivating the cause: it is like this—that one hears the six-syllable phrases.
Regarding the contemplation of the mind and the heart-veins, the six subtle methods are explained in detail, concluding with the statement:
"These are the six-syllable phrases of the Great Vīrya-Vīra-Ratnadhvaja.

Third, regarding the explanation of the six sense faculties through the six-syllable phrases: starting from Śāriputra’s presence in the Śītavana forest, when Sona asked about the eye—how one who is associated with the eye and forms should maintain restraint—the six sense faculties are explained in detail.
The conclusion subsequently states:
"Hearing these six characters and phrases, one practices the method of counting the breath and binding the mindfulness for pure conduct.
This refers precisely to the three types of arising and ceasing; since the textual meaning is clear and distinct, I have relied upon this as the criterion for judgment.
First, regarding the six-character phrases that clarify the six realms: the six realms are phenomena of karmic retribution; therefore, the six realms constitute the six-character gate.
Within each single realm, there are further distinguished infinite varieties, which are the "phrases."
Avalokiteśvara further contemplates the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the six realms of existence and attains the ultimate goal of the *dhāraṇī*.
As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Regarding the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*), is there a self therein or not?"
He replied:
"There is a self.

This self is precisely the Buddha-nature; because the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have thoroughly investigated this principle of nature, they have attained mastery among all paths. Therefore, by means of the power of dhāraṇī, they are able to eliminate the poisonous harms of the three obstructions within the six realms of existence.

In this present verse, only the names of the five destinies are listed; however, according to the traditional interpretation of the five destinies, if the asuras are combined with the hungry ghosts, they constitute a single destiny, whereas if they are separated, they form six destinies.
The current text clearly identifies the asura realm as one path;
it further mentions the realm of hungry ghosts but does not distinguish the heavenly realm. Is this due to an omission by the translator, or is there some other underlying intention?
Now, those who deliberate on this matter may suggest that the Way of Heaven is too meager to be discussed, as it merely clarifies the five lower realms; therefore, they do not treat the sixth.
Furthermore, within the prose sections [of the sūtras], there is indeed the principle of six realms.
Why is this? It is like a cloud drifting from a lost path, or even as a woman undergoes the pains of childbirth; such is the human realm.
This mantra is majestic and sublime, capable of delivering one from the sufferings of the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, and asuras—namely, the four evil paths.
Regarding the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*): the long-lived heavens constitute one difficulty; this term encompasses the heavenly realm, and thus all six destinies are included.
Furthermore, the verse states: "Universally instructing all beings, causing them to leave behind the suffering of birth and death."
If that is so, then the term "all" encompasses the six realms of existence, and so forth.
Now, within this section concerning the six realms, there are four parts:
first, clarifying the removal of the hardships and afflictions of the six realms; second, clarifying gain and loss; third, the recitation of verses; and fourth, the conclusion, as per the text.
That all inauspicious matters of this life and future lives are forever exhausted without remainder is the loss of light;
that one is fully endowed with the diligence of upholding the precepts is the attainment of light.
Furthermore, there are two meanings:
first, it clarifies that one attains mindfulness, concentration, and the dhāraṇī of all dharmas; second, it clarifies that one attains the vision of the Buddha and the *pratyāhāra-dhāraṇī*.
Regarding the attainment of this dhāraṇī, if one consults the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it is clear that the stage attained is equal to that of a Buddha.
As with the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), this is like the initial stage, and so forth.
Second, from the departure from Śrṇava in Rājagṛha, the six characters clarify the cultivation of causes.
This consists of two parts:
first, the general, and second, the specific.
Within the general section, there are again two parts:

First, regarding the brief contemplation of the heart and its channels: if explained according to the physical reality, it is simply the red flesh of the heart, the sovereign of the body; from these heart-channels, all other channels are able to open forth.

The mind capable of opening is the master of the body; from this mind-vein, all other veins can be opened and brought into circulation to form a single body, as described in detail in the *Sūtra on the Clear Observation* (Tōmyōkan), and so forth.
This is the explanation by way of causes and conditions.
If the meaning of the mind were empty, there would be nothing within the entire world that is not created from the mind.
The mind is like a skilled painter, creating the various five aggregates.
The various five aggregates exist because of the mind; because the mind is non-existent, all phenomena are also non-existent.
When the mind does not exist, all phenomena do not exist;
because the mind is empty, all phenomena are empty, and so forth.

Although all phenomena are empty, there exist various names for the channels as conventional designations; from the single channel of the mind to the infinite number of channels, one is able to penetrate them all without obstruction. This is because one realizes that the channel of the mind is a mere designation, and thus all phenomena are likewise mere designations, and so forth.
If the mind-pulse were definitively empty, emptiness could not be provisional;
if the mind were definitively provisional, the provisional could not be made empty.

One should know that the mind-pulse is neither empty nor provisional, and one should know that all pulses likewise are neither empty nor provisional. Thus, by negating the two extremes while simultaneously illuminating both emptiness and the provisional, this is precisely the perfect contemplation of the mind-pulse.
These three contemplations are applied across the ten types of practitioners, and so forth.

Now, regarding the formulation of the three contemplations based on the scriptural text: if there is one who can contemplate, there must be that which is contemplated; because the subject and object are joined, this is the contemplation of causes and conditions.
To cause the mind to contemplate a single point is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
To see Avalokiteśvara is the contemplation of provisional existence (*upāya*).
To immediately attain liberation is the contemplation of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*).

Furthermore, as for the statement that one "attains arhatship," this refers to the explanation of the arhat across the ten types of practitioners in both the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) and the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna); thus, there is no fault.
Second, from the passage beginning with "straightening the body" onwards, is the detailed explanation.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Based on the Dharma of Dhyāna," etc.,
the twenty-five kinds of skillful means each have both factual (事) and principled (理) interpretations. Here,
we specifically adopt the method of harmonizing the five factors to clarify the three skillful means of harmonizing the body, the breath, and the mind.
This is the intended meaning of the correct expedient means.

Tracing the origin of the physical body, it begins with three matters; because sentient beings do not know these three matters, they are called deluded, and because they realize these three matters, they are called awakened.
Now, in order to cultivate these six syllables, one must employ skillful means to harmonize these three matters:
straightening the body is the harmonization of the body; rectifying the mind is the harmonization of the mind; and the continuous flow of the mind and breath is the harmonization of the breath.
Uprightness of body pertains to ethical discipline (*śīla*); rectitude of mind pertains to meditative concentration (*samādhi*); and the continuity of the breath pertains to wisdom (*prajñā*).
This clarifies the harmonization of these three matters: ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
According to worldly convention, yang is above and yin is below, following secular custom.
As for placing yang on the right below and yin on the left above, this is intended to employ the method of stillness and stability to suppress the dispersal of yang.
Since worldly life possesses its own decorum, this is the use of the precepts (*śīla*) to restrain coarseness and ferocity; it corresponds to ethical discipline.

Second, regarding the active nature of the Yang and the quiescent nature of the Yin, using stillness to settle movement is the expedient means for subduing distraction; it corresponds to meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Third, the right side symbolizes expedient means (*upāya*), which belongs to the provisional and resides below; the left side represents true wisdom (*jñāna*), which resides above. This signifies manifesting the real from the provisional, which is precisely what symbolizes wisdom (*prajñā*).
These [practices of] morality, concentration, and wisdom are further explained in relation to ten types of practitioners, and so forth.
One raises the tongue toward the palate in order to prevent difficulties and to cease speech.
Counting from one to ten is the gate of counting.
Accomplishing mindfulness of breathing without directing it outward is the gate of following.
Being neither constricted nor lax, but balanced and harmonious, is the gate of settling.
The following section consists of three gates, as stated in the text.

From the "red flesh-heart" (*rakta-māṃsa-hṛdaya*), a single channel arises, which gives rise to four major channels leading to the four limbs; from each of these, ten channels arise, totaling forty channels.
Each of the four limbs has ten channels, from which a hundred further channels arise; together with the root channels, they total four hundred and forty.
For now, we shall speak only of the forty channels of the four limbs.
Furthermore, taking the ten channels of the head and combining them with the four fundamental channels, they are thus called the fourteen channels.
These extend from the tongue to the nose, analogous to the continuous flow between rivers and the ocean.
If the qi of the liver is green, the lungs white, the spleen yellow, and the kidneys black, yet only the heart is red and not visible, this is merely a brief description.
When the various qi gather at the nose, they lose their original colors; therefore, it is like lapis lazuli.
The breath is subtle and eight inches long; this also represents the transition from concentration toward dispersion, symbolizing the Eightfold Noble Path.
Within these Six Sublime Gates (Ṣaḍ-anupūrva-vihāra), there should generally be ten topical sections, but here we have only the "Gate of the Arising of a Single Characteristic."

If this "contemplation" (guan) refers to the general illumination contemplation, then from the point where the Buddha spoke of this "Great Perfection of Wisdom" (Mahāprajñāpāramitā) onwards, it specifically elucidates the Six Sublime Gates (liu miao men).
The preceding Six Sublime Gates are common to ordinary beings and shared by the Three Vehicles for their collective contemplation; therefore, they are called "general."
Since the three vehicles have not yet merged at present, one contemplates the six subtle gates separately.
First, regarding the explanation of the six subtle gates of the śrāvaka, there are two parts:
first, proceeding from great vigor, which is the praise of the six subtle gates.
From the words "Listen well, you all" onwards is the exhortation.
The text of the exhortation consists of two parts:
first, the exhortation; second, the acceptance and practice.
Now, regarding "illumination through exhortation": one should restrain the body and clarify the precepts; sitting upright in meditative absorption is concentration (*samādhi*).
Contemplating suffering is illumination through wisdom (*prajñā*).
As for suffering: this very retribution-body is a mass of suffering; from birth it has no master and is thus empty.
Because life comes to an end, it perishes; this is taken as the second [contemplation].
If impermanence is taken as the first, one contemplates the impermanence of mindfulness.
As for the five gates, there are three types of these:
First, the five points of stillness constitute the five gates, which is precisely the five-wheels dhyāna (*pañcacakradhyāna*).
This sutra states, "One should cause mindfulness to be fixed upon every joint," which is its meaning.
Second, the five methods of skillful means constitute the five-gate dhyāna.
Here, we clarify the single gate of mindfulness of the Buddha; the others are counting the breath, impurity, causal conditions, and loving-kindness.

However, the Abhidharma does not include mindfulness of the Buddha; it merely states that the "expedient means of the elements" (dhātu-upāya) serves to destroy the view of self, with the counting of breaths and so forth constituting the five gates.

Now, it is clarified that the expedient means of the elements is actually the contemplation of causes and conditions (hetu-pratyaya-vipaśyanā), which destroys views such as nihilism and eternalism; yet, because it still lacks mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Buddha and other practices are employed here to constitute the five gates.
The meaning of this is precisely what the text of this sutra states: "attaining the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha.
Third, the five gates of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and cessation are as presented in this very passage.
"Suffering, emptiness, and impermanence" is their meaning.
If the five wheels serve as the five gates, one is single-mindedly fixing mindfulness upon form; this belongs to meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
If impermanence and so forth serve as the five gates, one is single-mindedly engaging with principle; this is wisdom (*prajñā*).
If one employs the five expedient means, both concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are utilized together.

Furthermore, by expanding the contemplation for settling the mind (*pañca-vinodana*), one opens it into the Six Sublime Gates (*ṣaḍ-āyatana-mukha*); specifically, by expanding the expedient means of breath-counting (*ānāpāna*), one brings forth the two gates of following (*anugama*) and stopping (*sthiti*).

Why is this? There are three types of counting the breaths: combining the two skillful means of impurity and loving-kindness constitutes one gate of contemplation; the skillful means of causal conditions is the gate of returning; and mindfulness of the Buddha is the gate of purity.

Why is this so? Because in the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānusmṛti), there is the Dharma-body Buddha (dharmakāya-buddha), and the Dharma-body is precisely the purity of the principle of emptiness (śūnyatā).

Furthermore, the five expedient means (pañcopāya) and the six subtle gates (ṣaḍ-sūkṣma-dvāra) are combined into three obstacles: counting the breaths (ānāpāna-smṛti) pertains to the wind of retribution, and thus belongs to the obstacle of retribution (vipākāvaraṇa).
The three obstacles are treated by means of loving-kindness, impurity, and dependent origination, each having three aspects:

for example, counting the breath is a form of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*); since there are three types of applied and sustained thought, there are likewise three corresponding remedies, and so forth.

There are three kinds of anger: desire has internal and external aspects, and so forth; delusion has the nature of annihilationism and eternalism, and so forth; karma has floating and sinking states and evil objects, and so forth.
Correspondingly, there are also three methods for treating them, as detailed in the *Chanmen* [Treatise on the Meditation Gate], and so forth.

Now, this sutra does not employ such remedies; rather, it clarifies that all is empty, signless, like an illusion, and like a transformation, thereby entering the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) as a universal remedy, and so forth.
Second, "from the cold forest" refers to the practice of receiving and undertaking [the teachings].
Furthermore, there are two parts:
first, practicing with realization;
second, from "Sena heard" onwards, distinguishing the persons of the three vehicles through six gates.
The "cold forest" (śītavana) refers to the untainted (anāsrava) coolness.
Gold represents wisdom; because those of the three vehicles equally enter the principle of the ultimate dharma-nature (paramārtha-dharmatā), it is likened to gold.
Second, the question of Sna refers to the meaning of the third set of six-syllable phrases.
When the eye sees a form, there are three stages:
at the very first moment of thought, it is solitary ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*).
In a single thought-moment, it arises in conjunction with ignorance;
if it accords with form, it is craving; if it opposes it, it is aversion; if it is neutral, it gives rise to the indeterminate.
Regarding "abiding by encompassing the phenomena": this refers simply to counting the breaths so as not to allow the three types of mental activity to arise.

Regarding the discussion on principle: if one takes the sense organs and their objects as causes and conditions, and analyzes these causes and conditions part by part to perceive the principle through impermanence and arising-and-ceasing, this is like attaining the Way through the view of existence (*astitva*) as found in the *Abhidharma*.
If one contemplates that the sense faculties and their objects are pure, void, unreal, empty, and equal, seeing this principle is to see emptiness and attain the Way.
If one contemplates the sense faculties and their objects as the causal conditions of ignorance, volitional formations, old age, and death, such a person is a pratyekabuddha.
There is no logical error in grouping these six faculties together without following their sequential order.

When it is now stated that visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility are associated with the subtle and smooth, the five faculties are subtle and are all subsumed within the body faculty and mental objects (*dharmas*).

When the mind-faculty perceives mental objects (dharmas), the body already exists in a state of potentiality as various tactile sensations arrive; therefore, it is said that visible forms, odors, and so forth are associated with the subtle and smooth, for the "subtle and smooth" is the body itself.
The six sense organs are treated as an analogy for the principle; the meanings of the Shared, Distinct, and Perfect [teachings] are as follows.
Regarding "the earth has no solidity": it is said that there is no solidity because it is according to reality (*yathābhūta*).
In the Shared Teaching, one contemplates the earth as being like an illusion or a reflection in a mirror.
There are four propositions regarding "solidity": to scrutinize the subtle principle of atoms (paramāṇu) and regard them as existent is "solidity";
to view them as empty is the "view of non-existence.
Even to be deeply attached to these four propositions such that they cannot be relinquished is all termed "solidity."
Now, these four attachments are swept away and these four faults are eliminated because [the self] cannot be found when sought.
It is said that earth has no solidity because water does not abide within the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
As for wind having no obstruction, how could it lack the four propositions regarding substantial obstruction?

Regarding this body emitting fire: those liberated through wisdom possess only the fire of the untainted (*anāsrava*), whereas those liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*) possess both the fires of phenomena and principle.
Those with wisdom burn the cause of the body’s bondage—the fetters of the seeds—while those liberated both ways burn the result of the body’s bondage—the fruits of the fetters.

To see the Buddhas of the ten directions is the stage of a śrāvaka; to destroy evil and become a pratyekabuddha is the stage of a pratyekabuddha; to abide in non-retrogression is the stage of a bodhisattva.
The term "clad" (fu) serves to conclude the intended meaning.
